abstract: A critical, annotated version of Narlikar’s iconic novel about a cybervirus attack by an advanced alien species—with updated text and added material. A year before Robin Cook’s Invasion (1997)—in which an alien force activates a latent biological virus in humans—and almost a decade before Liu Cixin’s The Remembrance of Earth’s Past trilogy (2008–2010)—in which humanity’s scientific progress is curtailed by an alien supercomputer’s “sophon-lock”—Jayant Vishnu Narlikar’s Virus (1996) painted a similar scenario. In his novel, a cybervirus broadcast by an advanced, extraterrestrial species invades Earth and freezes its digital infrastructure: a prelude to an alien invasion. The novel, first published in Marathi, recounts how vast radio arrays on Earth intercept a seemingly innocuous message from an unknown planet orbiting Barnard’s Star. The radio signal, sent six years prior, coalesces into a cybervirus that has the potential to cause a complete digital meltdown and lead humanity into an age of chaos—an alien first strike to prevent humanity from evolving further. This book—a critical, annotated version of Virus, edited and revised by Sami Ahmad Khan—reissues Narlikar’s iconic novel with updated text and added dimensions. It includes detailed annotations that locate the technology of the text along the axis of contemporary scientific thought, as well as critical essays that focus on the literary, political, and sociocultural dimensions of the novel; essays on Narlikar’s role in India’s science and science fiction; an exclusive conversation with the author; bibliographical information on his works; and a bonus short story. Contributions by Sami Ahmad Khan, Nilam Ingole, Priteegandha Naik, Jayant V. Narlikar, and Dibyadyuti Roy.

title: Beyond Viral Pathogenesis: Climate Change, Zoonotic Spillover, and the Evolving Epidemiology of Viral Hemorrhagic Fevers
abstract: Viral hemorrhagic fevers (VHFs) represent a major global health threat because they can cause severe systemic illness, hemorrhage, multiorgan dysfunction, and death. Ebola virus, Marburg virus, Lassa virus, and Crimean–Congo hemorrhagic fever virus contribute substantially to the global burden of these diseases. These pathogens employ diverse transmission routes, including vector-borne transmission, zoonotic spillover, and direct exposure to infected bodily fluids. Climate change, land use alterations, urbanization, population growth, and increased human–animal interactions may reshape pathogen ecology and create new opportunities for viral emergence and transmission. International travel and interconnected human populations further complicate outbreak containment. This review examines the pathophysiological mechanisms, epidemiological patterns, and major outbreaks associated with VHFs, with particular emphasis on how environmental change, ecological disruption, and infectious disease dynamics interact. We also evaluate the roles of global health organizations in strengthening disease surveillance, coordinating outbreak responses, and promoting international preparedness. Furthermore, we discuss the importance of integrated surveillance systems, cross-sectoral collaboration, and climate-informed public health strategies in reducing the risks associated with emerging and recurring VHF outbreaks. By integrating virological, ecological, epidemiological, and public health perspectives, this review highlights critical knowledge gaps and identifies priorities for improving early detection, outbreak preparedness, and coordinated responses to future VHF threats.

title: Targeting host eIF4A with zotatifin inhibits Bundibugyo virus and other filoviruses
abstract: Filoviruses, including Ebola and Marburg viruses, depend on host eIF4A helicase activity for replication. Zotatifin is a first in class, clinical stage eIF4A inhibitor that acts as a molecular glue, stabilizing the interaction between eIF4A and selected polypurine rich RNA sequences, thereby inhibiting RNA unwinding and ribosomal scanning. Here, we identify pronounced polypurine enrichment in the 5'untranslated regions (5'UTRs) of the seven major filoviral protein-coding genes NP, VP35, VP40, GP, VP30, VP24, and L across four virus species, including Bundibugyo virus (BDBV). Consistent with these findings, zotatifin inhibits the replication of Ebola, Marburg, Sudan, Tai Forest, and Bundibugyo viruses at low nanomolar concentrations. Zotatifin has been administered to humans in oncology and COVID19 clinical studies. Clinical pharmacokinetic pharmacodynamic (PKPD) modeling indicates that exposures resulting in inhibition of BDBV replication are achievable in humans at tolerated doses following subcutaneous administration. Together, these findings support the repurposing of zotatifin as a host directed antiviral candidate against BDBV and other filoviruses, with potential applications in preparedness for future outbreaks.

title: Quantifying the extinction probability of Marburg virus disease outbreaks: A continuous-time Markov chain model integrating a multi-type branching process
abstract: Understanding the extinction dynamics of Marburg virus disease is crucial, particularly during the early stages of an outbreak when stochastic effects strongly influence disease outcomes. Although deterministic models have provided valuable insights into virus transmission dynamics, they cannot adequately capture random transmission events or quantify extinction probabilities, particularly when outbreaks begin with few infected cases. This study develops a continuous-time Markov chain stochastic model derived from a deterministic multi-host transmission model. The model incorporates a multi-type branching process, in which distinct infectious types are tracked according to their contributions to secondary infections, enabling estimation of disease extinction probabilities during the early outbreak phase. The extinction analysis shows that outbreaks initiated by exposed humans have a higher probability of extinction (21.6%) compared with those initiated by infectious humans (13.7%), whereas outbreaks initiated by infected bats have an extinction probability of only 0.36%, highlighting their role as important reservoirs sustaining virus transmission. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that reducing human-to-human transmission, decreasing viral shedding, and increasing environmental viral decay significantly enhance the likelihood of disease extinction. The proposed framework provides a quantitative tool for assessing Marburg virus disease outbreak risk and valuable insights for designing early interventions for human transmission, environmental contamination, and cross-species interactions.

title_zh: 量化马尔堡病毒病 暴发的灭绝概率:一种整合多类型分支过程的连续时间马尔可夫链模型
source_body_en: Understanding the extinction dynamics of Marburg virus disease is crucial, particularly during the early stages of an outbreak when stochastic effects strongly influence disease outcomes. Although deterministic models have provided valuable insights into virus transmission dynamics, they cannot adequately capture random transmission events or quantify extinction probabilities, particularly when outbreaks begin with few infected cases. This study develops a continuous-time Markov chain stochastic model derived from a deterministic multi-host transmission model. The model incorporates a multi-type branching process, in which distinct infectious types are tracked according to their contributions to secondary infections, enabling estimation of disease extinction probabilities during the early outbreak phase. The extinction analysis shows that outbreaks initiated by exposed humans have a higher probability of extinction (21.6%) compared with those initiated by infectious humans (13.7%), whereas outbreaks initiated by infected bats have an extinction probability of only 0.36%, highlighting their role as important reservoirs sustaining virus transmission. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that reducing human-to-human transmission, decreasing viral shedding, and increasing environmental viral decay significantly enhance the likelihood of disease extinction. The proposed framework provides a quantitative tool for assessing Marburg virus disease outbreak risk and valuable insights for designing early interventions for human transmission, environmental contamination, and cross-species interactions.
abstract_zh: 理解马尔堡病毒病的灭绝动力学至关重要,尤其是在暴发初期阶段,随机效应对疾病结果有显著影响。尽管确定性模型为病毒传播动力学提供了有价值的见解,但它们无法充分捕捉随机传播事件或量化灭绝概率,特别是在暴发初始病例较少时。本研究基于一个确定性多宿主 传播模型,开发了一个连续时间马尔可夫链随机模型。该模型采用多类型分支过程,根据不同感染类型对二次感染的贡献进行追踪,从而能够在暴发初期阶段估计疾病灭绝概率。灭绝分析表明,由暴露人类引发的暴发灭绝概率为21.6%,高于由传染性人类引发的暴发(13.7%),而由感染蝙蝠引发的暴发灭绝概率仅为0.36%,突显了蝙蝠作为重要储存宿主维持病毒传播的作用。此外,研究结果表明,减少人传人传播、降低病毒排毒量以及增加环境病毒衰减显著提高了疾病灭绝的可能性。所提出的框架为评估马尔堡病毒病 暴发风险提供了定量工具,并为设计针对人类传播、环境污染和跨物种互动的早期干预措施提供了有价值的见解。

full_text: Abstract Introduction In regions with a high malaria burden, overlapping symptoms, such as fever, complicate case detection, surveillance, and response to outbreaks of Ebola Virus Disease (EVD). During the 2022 Ebola Sudan Virus Disease (SVD) outbreak in Uganda’s Mubende and Kassanda districts, clinically differentiating febrile illnesses proved challenging and potentially delayed Ebola case identification and increased exposure risk. This paper documents stakeholders’ perceptions of the contribution of, and the facilitators and barriers to, Mass Drug Administration (MDA) for malaria during the outbreak in Mubende and Kassanda districts, Uganda. Methods This was a qualitative descriptive study involving 30 key informant interviews with health workers, local leaders, and implementers alongside 10 focus group discussions with community members and community health workers (CHWs). Data were transcribed, translated, and thematically analyzed.
